analysis.one_liner: Shuts down the Export-Import Bank, ending taxpayer-backed loans, guarantees, and insurance for exports.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by one House Republican with 7 cosponsors, never got a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Export-Import Bank is a government agency that helps U.S. companies sell abroad by issuing loans, loan guarantees, and insurance backed by taxpayers. This bill would have stopped the bank from taking new applications within 30 days, wound down its existing obligations over time, and abolished it three years after enactment, with the Treasury Department handling the wind-down. The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would no longer stand behind export financing through federal guarantees; U.S. businesses that compete against firms receiving export subsidies; and private lenders that already provide trade finance at market rates.

how_it_helps.text: The bank would stop accepting new applications for loans, insurance, or guarantees 30 days after enactment, and would be abolished entirely three years later, with remaining obligations wound down by the Treasury Secretary.
The bill's findings state that most of the bank's financing subsidizes exports of large multinational corporations rather than the small businesses it cites as its mission.

The bill cites a June 2012 Congressional Budget Office analysis finding that the bank's expected return under fair-value accounting was less than a tenth of what official scoring methods estimate, arguing taxpayers bear more risk than official accounting shows.

The bill's findings state that banks and other financial institutions profit from the bank's loan guarantees and trade insurance, and that private markets already supply trade finance at competitive rates.

analysis.who_pays: Large exporters that rely on the bank's financing and insurance, the banks that earn fees administering its guarantees, and some small-business exporters that use its credit insurance would lose access to the subsidized financing. Foreign buyers of U.S. goods financed through the bank would also lose that credit channel.

drawbacks.text: Exporters that depend on the bank would lose a financing option that private markets may not fully replace, while foreign governments continue financing their own exporters through official export-credit agencies, potentially leaving U.S. sellers at a disadvantage.
Some small businesses do use the bank's export credit insurance, and the bill's own findings acknowledge the bank claims to serve small businesses; ending it removes that tool for them too.
The bank has historically operated at a surplus under official accounting, so ending it would forgo that income even as it removes risk from the federal balance sheet.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is that a government agency is extending subsidized credit that mostly benefits large corporations and the banks that administer its guarantees, with taxpayer risk understated by official accounting. The strongest objection is that other governments subsidize their exporters, so unilateral abolition could cost U.S. export sales. The bill handled the transition more carefully than an immediate shutdown — a 30-day cutoff on new applications, a 12-month cutoff on new contracts, and a Treasury-run wind-down of existing obligations — which addresses the disruption concern but does not address the foreign-subsidy argument.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Financial Services Committee from March 2019 onward, never got a committee vote or floor action, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Justin Amash introduced the Export-Import Bank Termination Act on March 27, 2019, joined by five original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the day it was introduced.
Seven Republicans cosponsored the bill in total.
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no committee markup, no floor vote, no Senate action — for the remainder of the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Export-Import Bank and the exporters and banks that depend on its financing are better off, because the agency kept operating and continued issuing export financing for the rest of the Congress. The bill's sponsors and the taxpayers they sought to shield gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bank, its exporters, and its partner banks

for.name: Justin Amash
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to abolish the Export-Import Bank on March 27, 2019.

for.name: 7 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote after it was referred; the record shows no committee action.

against.name: Exporters and banks reliant on Ex-Im financing
against.role: Export-credit program users, led by large manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Have historically organized and lobbied to preserve and reauthorize the Export-Import Bank, whose financing supports their export sales and fee income.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Republicans, but no vote was ever taken to reveal where the parties stood; historically, support for the bank has crossed party lines, with business-oriented members of both parties backing it.

industries.note: The bill's findings state that most of the bank's financing subsidizes exports of large multinational corporations. Keeping the bank keeps a taxpayer-backed subsidy flowing to firms that compete at home against unsubsidized businesses.
Banks earn fees administering the bank's guarantees and insurance, but they also face competition from its direct loans; the bill would end both the fee stream and the competition.
The bill's findings argue export subsidies advantage specific industries at the expense of their domestic competition; abolition would end that advantage.
